lessons.name: HBM layer count and physical height
lessons.shortName: HBM layer count and physical height
lessons.role: Separate memory-die count, package thickness, stored bits and interface bandwidth.
lessons.description: An HBM stack is assembled from separately fabricated DRAM dies and a base/interface structure. “12-high” describes a specified count of memory dies; it is neither twelve transistors nor a height in micrometers. Within a mechanical envelope, adding layers requires redistributing the thickness budget among silicon, inter-die joints, base structures and clearance. Wafer thinning and TSV reveal make vertical electrical paths accessible, but thin dies are harder to handle without bow or damage. Capacity rises with the number of usable bits in the memory dies. External bandwidth is set by the interface and achievable data rate, so more dies do not automatically create more external signal wires.
mechanism: Begin with tested memory wafers and identify whether each drawing counts memory dies or the base die.
Thin on a compatible carrier; measure total thickness variation, warp and TSV reveal before handling the separated dies.
Allocate a mechanical budget to the base, every silicon layer, every counted bond line and the top allowance.
Verify that pad positions, channels, thermal path and package interfaces remain compatible as the layer count changes.
Test the assembled stack and report capacity, bandwidth and physical height as three separate outcomes.

science.title: Stack-height budget
science.equation: H = tbase + N tdie + J tbond + tcap
science.explanation: Count each physical thickness once. J includes every bond line represented in this cross-section; its value depends on whether the base interface is included.
science.assumptions: Uniform die/bond thickness is a teaching simplification. Real layouts include local steps, tolerances and route-specific top structures.

science.title: Capacity is not bandwidth
science.equation: C = N Cdie; B = w r η / 8
science.explanation: Capacity C counts bytes; bandwidth B counts delivered bytes each second across the stated interface.
science.assumptions: Equal capacity dies; data rate r already counts transfers; usable efficiency must be stated.

specs.label: Layer count
specs.context: Read each product drawing’s counting convention.

specs.label: Height budget
specs.context: A die-count label is not a dimensional drawing.

interfaces.name: TSV reveal
interfaces.signal: Exposed vertical conductors and measured silicon thickness

interfaces.name: Accelerator package
interfaces.signal: Stack height, interface footprint and thermal contact

lessons.tradeoff: Thinner silicon frees vertical space while increasing handling sensitivity; smaller joints demand tighter assembly control.
lessons.whyAI: A larger working set can fit locally without a proportional increase in external memory bandwidth.
lessons.misconception: Die count, silicon thickness and the external interface are separate design variables.

check.question: A stack changes from 8 to 12 memory dies at unchanged external width and pin rate. What follows directly?
options: Capacity can rise; external peak bandwidth need not change
External bandwidth must rise by 50%
Physical height must rise by 50%
check.explanation: Die count, silicon thickness and the external interface are separate design variables.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic budget: base 60 µm, 12 memory dies × 30 µm, 12 included joints × 7 µm and a 40 µm allowance give 544 µm. Changing die thickness to 40 µm gives 664 µm. These are arithmetic inputs, not a JEDEC height limit or product cross-section.
lessons.evidenceNotes: SK hynix’s 2023 account describes fitting more DRAM dies into the same height through thinner dies and changed assembly. The source supports the mechanism; the lab uses independent illustrative dimensions.

lessons.name: HBM heat, assembly yield and test access
lessons.shortName: HBM heat, assembly yield and test access
lessons.role: Explain how added layers affect the heat path, screening strategy and delivered good stacks.
lessons.description: Every added die introduces heat sources, interfaces and opportunities for assembly damage. Heat follows several parallel paths through silicon, metal, polymer and the surrounding package; the hottest location is not necessarily the tallest die. Test coverage changes with access: a wafer test can inspect some die functions before stacking, while TSV chains, cross-die connections and the complete high-speed interface require later checks. A known-good input is a unit that passed a defined screen, not a physically perfect die. Assembly yield therefore starts from screened inputs and counts newly introduced failures, avoiding a second charge for the same wafer loss.
mechanism: Define incoming wafer/die test coverage and preserve identity through thinning, singulation and stacking.
Measure continuity and functional behavior at the stages where test access exists; map errors to the same stack genealogy.
Estimate heat from each active layer using a stated power distribution and boundary temperature.
Inspect assembly defects with electrical tests plus suitable imaging; a hot spot or open circuit alone does not identify its cause.
Separate per-unit screening, product reliability qualification and observed in-service failure rates.

science.title: Multiple heat sources
science.explanation: A thermal-resistance matrix represents how each heat source j contributes to temperature at location i, including cross-heating.
science.assumptions: Linear steady-state approximation at specified boundaries. Transients and temperature-dependent properties require a richer model.

science.title: Conditional assembly yield
science.explanation: J is the number of independently modeled assembly interfaces, each with aggregate conditional pass probability yjoint.
science.assumptions: Screened inputs; excludes residual input escapes, correlated defects, repair and common tooling failures. An interface probability is not a per-bump probability.

specs.label: Yield denominator
specs.context: Do not multiply their original wafer yield a second time.

specs.label: Thermal boundary
specs.context: Stack-average temperature can hide local limits.

interfaces.name: Die screening
interfaces.signal: Coverage, bin and residual escape risk

interfaces.name: Stack test
interfaces.signal: Functional, interconnect and thermal evidence

lessons.tradeoff: Earlier screening avoids wasting downstream components, but adds handling, test time and cost; some failures are only observable after assembly.
lessons.whyAI: Effective stack supply and sustainable frequency depend on both manufacturability and thermal operation.
lessons.misconception: Track the denominator at each stage; conditional assembly loss acts on the units that actually enter assembly.

check.question: Why not multiply wafer yield into every already screened die again?
options: It double-counts losses already excluded from the incoming population
Screening guarantees zero future failures
HBM assembly cannot introduce faults
check.explanation: Track the denominator at each stage; conditional assembly loss acts on the units that actually enter assembly.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic independent-interface model: 12 interfaces at 99.5% conditional pass probability yield about 94.2%; at 99.9%, about 98.8%. A shared contamination event violates independence. These values do not estimate any supplier’s yield.
lessons.evidenceNotes: imec’s 2025 thermal study concerns a specified research HBM-on-GPU arrangement. It motivates spatial heat analysis; its simulated temperatures are not general product limits.

lessons.name: Thermocompression with non-conductive film
lessons.role: Trace a bump-based TC-NCF route and separate polymer behavior from electrical contact formation.
lessons.description: Thermocompression bonding applies controlled temperature, force and alignment to form interconnections. In a TC-NCF route, a non-conductive film occupies the space between the mating dies while metallic bumps and pads carry the electrical connection. The polymer must deform and cure without blocking intended contacts or trapping unacceptable voids. Thin-die handling, film behavior and bump geometry are therefore coupled. TC-NCF is one thermocompression implementation, not a synonym for every bump process or every adhesive. Samsung’s February 2024 HBM3E 12H announcement gives a concrete historical application; it does not make one vendor’s process window universal.
mechanism: Prepare bumped dies, compatible film and verified surface/handling conditions.
Place the film at its defined wafer or die stage; maintain the intended contact openings and contamination controls.
Align a die to the receiving die and apply the qualified thermal/force cycle for metallic contact and polymer flow/cure.
Repeat the specified stacking sequence while tracking placement error and cumulative warpage.
Inspect continuity, bond-line condition and voids; complete the product-specific reliability qualification.

science.title: Serial tool occupancy
science.explanation: This estimates occupied tool time for a strictly serial die-placement/bonding sequence.
science.assumptions: No overlapping stations or batch operations. It is not factory cycle time, and route-specific curing may occupy different equipment.

specs.label: Electrical path
specs.context: NCF itself is electrically insulating.

specs.label: Control variables
specs.value: Alignment, force, thermal cycle and film state
specs.context: Values are recipe- and material-specific, not supplied here.

interfaces.name: Prepared die and film
interfaces.signal: Surface, metallurgy, rheology and alignment

interfaces.name: Bonded die pair
interfaces.signal: Electrical joints and cured/processed polymer interface

lessons.tradeoff: Sequential local bonding provides process control but tool occupancy, film flow and thin-die stress must close together.
lessons.whyAI: A packaging decision changes manufacturable stack height, test yield and the number of usable HBM stacks delivered.
lessons.misconception: NCF supplies insulation and mechanical support; metal joints provide the conductive path.

check.question: In TC-NCF, what carries current between memory dies?
options: The metallic interconnections
The non-conductive film
The surrounding air gap
check.explanation: NCF supplies insulation and mechanical support; metal joints provide the conductive path.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic serial flow: 12 placements × (0.3 s alignment + 0.7 s bonding) plus 3 s handling occupy 15 s. A different station layout could overlap work; this calculation predicts neither commercial throughput nor yield.
lessons.evidenceNotes: Historical vendor example: Samsung reported an advanced TC-NCF route for its 2024 HBM3E 12H development. Sampling, qualification and volume production are distinct statuses.

lessons.name: Mass reflow and molded underfill
lessons.role: Separate stack placement, metallic reflow and molding in an MR-MUF assembly route.
lessons.description: Mass reflow forms many solder interconnections within a thermal operation. Molded underfill subsequently fills and encapsulates the intended spaces with molding compound. The route therefore separates electrical joint formation from the bulk protective fill, although particular implementations can use additional stabilization during stacking. Polymer flow through narrow gaps, trapped gas, die bow and reflow behavior still matter. Increasing the number of parts processed together can move a bottleneck from the bond operation to alignment, molding, cure, inspection or test; a batch label does not establish the final factory output.
mechanism: Align and place the compatible bumped memory dies while controlling thin-die shape.
Apply any stabilization required by the named implementation; do not assume all MR-MUF products share this substep.
Run the selected reflow operation to connect the metallic joints across the assembled stack.
Fill and encapsulate using the specified molded-underfill sequence; control venting, flow, pressure and cure.
Inspect the same traced stack for joint continuity, voiding, warpage and functional behavior.

science.title: Batch-limited station rate
science.explanation: K is processed stacks per batch and a is the productive-time fraction. Q is the station’s nominal processed-stack rate before yield.
science.assumptions: Consistent time units, full modeled batch, no double counting overlap; the slowest compatible route station can dominate the line.

specs.label: Reflow
specs.context: Do not describe polymer encapsulation as the conductor.

specs.label: Molded underfill
specs.context: Flow, voids and mechanical behavior require separate controls.

interfaces.name: Placed bump stack
interfaces.signal: Alignment and solderable interfaces

interfaces.name: Encapsulated stack
interfaces.signal: Connected and mechanically supported memory

lessons.tradeoff: Batch processing can reduce per-stack occupancy at one station while narrow-gap filling, alignment and inspection determine end-to-end yield and capacity.
lessons.whyAI: Memory demand becomes qualified delivered stacks only after the whole assembly route can sustain its required rate.
lessons.misconception: Factory output follows the limiting compatible stage, including its yield and availability.

check.question: A reflow station doubles its rate while molding remains slower. What happens to line capacity?
options: It can remain limited by molding
It necessarily doubles
It becomes independent of test time
check.explanation: Factory output follows the limiting compatible stage, including its yield and availability.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic station: 20 stacks per 100 s batch at 80% productive time gives 0.16 stacks/s, or 576 stacks/hour before yield. A 400-stack/hour downstream screen caps this toy line below the reflow rate.
lessons.evidenceNotes: SK hynix’s process explanation describes reflow and molded underfill as separate roles, with implementation-specific chip stabilization in its advanced route. No comparative vendor yield or cost is assumed.

lessons.name: Hybrid bonding: surface-to-interface closure
lessons.role: Follow CMP, cleaning, alignment, contact and anneal as one surface-controlled integration problem.
lessons.description: Hybrid bonding joins a dielectric interface together with matching conductive pads. The goal is a dense direct connection without a solder-bump gap at that interface. Surface flatness alone is insufficient: local copper topography, surface chemistry, particles, placement error and the thermal cycle determine whether the two material systems can join as intended. A wafer-to-wafer process and a die-to-wafer process have different handling, selection and throughput constraints. A successful research pitch demonstration establishes a result on its specified test structure; it does not establish that a complete HBM product is shipping with that process.
mechanism: Form patterned bonding metal and dielectric, then planarize to a controlled local topography.
Measure copper recess, surface roughness and within-wafer variation; clean and prepare the bonding surfaces.
For a die route, preserve the prepared surface through singulation and handling; retain the known-good input map.
Align and contact according to the chosen route, then complete the required anneal for the bonded interface.
Assess electrical chains, voids, alignment and mechanical integrity, and qualify the full product separately.

science.title: Geometric pad-overlap example
science.explanation: For equal square pads, misalignment reduces geometrical overlap in both axes. Electrical yield also depends on surface and material behavior.
science.assumptions: Rigid planar equal squares; no rotation, deformation or local overlay field. This is not a qualified bond tolerance.

specs.label: Surface condition
specs.context: A mean wafer flatness value cannot certify every bond interface.

specs.label: Route distinction
specs.context: Do not transfer one route’s pitch/throughput claim to the other.

interfaces.name: Prepared metal/dielectric surface
interfaces.signal: Measured topography, cleanliness and pad position

interfaces.name: Bonded interface
interfaces.signal: Electrical, dielectric and mechanical continuity

lessons.tradeoff: Finer direct interconnects can reduce spacing, but surface preparation, handling and overlay increase integration demands; solder self-alignment cannot be assumed.
lessons.whyAI: The available interface pitch and thermal/mechanical envelope constrain future memory-on-logic arrangements.
lessons.misconception: Bond success depends on local conditions and the integrated route; one average cannot settle all failure mechanisms.

check.question: A clean-looking surface has acceptable mean flatness. Is that sufficient evidence of good hybrid bonds?
options: No: local topography, chemistry, alignment and bonded-interface tests remain necessary
Yes: average flatness certifies all electrical connections
Yes: annealing removes every particle
check.explanation: Bond success depends on local conditions and the integrated route; one average cannot settle all failure mechanisms.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic equal square pads of width 2 µm offset 0.2 µm in x and y retain 3.24 µm² overlap, 81% of the nominal area. This geometric result is neither an 81% bond yield nor a recommended pad design.
lessons.evidenceNotes: imec sources establish wafer-to-wafer and die-to-wafer research mechanisms. Product-specific HBM hybrid-bond qualification, throughput and cost are not inferred.

lessons.name: Selecting a bonding route under constraints
lessons.shortName: Selecting a bonding route under constraints
lessons.role: Compare qualified output, height, thermal behavior, inspection and cost on the same product boundary.
lessons.description: A useful process comparison starts from one required product: die count, footprint, electrical interfaces, operating conditions and test coverage. TC-NCF, MR-MUF and hybrid bonding organize joint formation and support differently. Each route moves effort among surface preparation, die placement, joint formation, encapsulation, annealing and inspection. “Finer pitch” and “faster bond tool” are individual attributes, not complete cost or delivery answers. Keep development readiness and demonstrated results beside each route, and leave supplier yield, process time or commercial price unknown when undisclosed.
mechanism: Fix the same functional memory requirement and package-height boundary before comparing alternatives.
Map the chosen route’s preparation, handling, bonding/fill, thermal and test steps without replacing them with one generic bond operation.
Define compatible station capacity and conditional yield for the same input population.
Include consumables, equipment occupancy, inspection and losses in a cost per accepted stack model.
Reject or revise routes that miss electrical, thermal, mechanical or qualification requirements even if nominal throughput is high.

science.title: Cost per accepted stack
science.explanation: Costs are normalized to one assembled input set and divided by final pass fraction.
science.assumptions: Simple no-rework average with all modeled costs incurred per input set; stage-dependent scrap/rework requires a yield waterfall.

specs.label: Comparison basis
specs.context: Different layer counts or qualification stages are not an equal comparison.

specs.label: Readiness
specs.context: Keep date and measured scope visible.

interfaces.name: Process candidate
interfaces.signal: Flow, equipment and material requirements

interfaces.name: Integration decision
interfaces.signal: Feasible route plus remaining evidence needs

lessons.tradeoff: Reducing joint thickness can consume more surface-control effort; reducing bond time may expose inspection or supply as the next bottleneck.
lessons.whyAI: Memory economics and supply depend on accepted output from the complete route, affecting how many accelerators can be deployed.
lessons.misconception: A process must close the full product and production requirements; one favorable parameter does not establish a usable stack.

check.question: Which comparison supports an engineering choice?
options: Same product boundary, yield denominator and qualification requirements
Only minimum reported pitch
Only the fastest advertised bonding operation
check.explanation: A process must close the full product and production requirements; one favorable parameter does not establish a usable stack.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic routes: 100 currency units per input set at 90% final yield cost 111.1 per accepted stack. A 105-unit route at 97% costs 108.2. The example illustrates sensitivity; it ranks no commercial process.
lessons.evidenceNotes: Route mechanisms are grounded in their named sources. Cost, cycle time and yield values in the workbench are transparent teaching scenarios, not supplier disclosures.

lessons.name: HBF: a read-oriented tier and its evidence boundary
lessons.shortName: HBF: a read-oriented tier and its evidence boundary
lessons.role: Distinguish an announced HBF interface/capacity specification from validated workload behavior.
lessons.description: High Bandwidth Flash proposes a NAND-based tier near the processor, alongside the existing memory hierarchy. SK hynix’s August 2026 announcement describes up to 512 GB and bandwidth grades of approximately 0.4–3.0 TB/s, with UCIe connectivity. These are reported specification boundaries, not proof of sustained throughput on a deployed inference system. A capacity and read-bandwidth headline leaves access latency, request granularity, concurrency, write service and host software to be examined. NAND-based capacity can be attractive for read-heavy state, but it does not acquire DRAM semantics merely by sharing a package or a fast link.
mechanism: Identify the source date and distinguish technical specification, sample, qualified component and shipping system.
Map the processor link, HBF controller and NAND array as separate interfaces; use the same transfer direction and byte convention.
Request latency, granularity, concurrency and read/write conditions before treating the headline rate as usable.
Keep mutable working state and recovery requirements in the placement contract rather than assuming every tensor can move to flash.
Measure application-level correctness, latency and energy on a named integration before claiming a deployment benefit.

science.title: Minimum bulk-read transfer time
science.explanation: Moving V payload bytes cannot take less than V/B at usable bandwidth B, even before initial access, scheduling or contention.
science.assumptions: Single direction with compatible decimal units; B is a sustained payload assumption, not automatically an advertised interface maximum.

specs.label: Evidence snapshot
specs.context: Reported specification: up to 512 GB; grades approximately 0.4–3.0 TB/s.

specs.label: Interface
specs.context: A common framework is not a drop-in compatibility or shipped-system certificate.

specs.label: Still configuration-dependent
specs.context: The headline grades do not settle end-to-end service performance.

interfaces.name: Processor/HBF interface
interfaces.signal: Requests, completion, error and transfer semantics

interfaces.name: NAND-backed capacity
interfaces.signal: Data with specified access and persistence behavior

lessons.tradeoff: More near-compute capacity may reduce remote movement, while page access, writes and integration requirements can move the performance bottleneck.
lessons.whyAI: Large read-mostly parameter pools are a possible use case; they require a software and system plan that accounts for access behavior.
lessons.misconception: An interface/specification announcement and a measured shipping-system result are different evidence states.

check.question: What does the announced HBF bandwidth range establish?
options: A reported specification range that still needs workload validation
Guaranteed HBM-equivalent random-access latency
Proof that every GPU can attach HBF today
check.explanation: An interface/specification announcement and a measured shipping-system result are different evidence states.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic payload-only calculation: reading 100 GB at an assumed sustained 1 TB/s requires at least 0.1 s. No setup, concurrency loss or other work is included. The assumed usable rate is not a measured HBF benchmark.
lessons.evidenceNotes: SK hynix and Sandisk identify the August 2026 milestone as specification release. The atlas has not verified a volume-shipping deployment from these announcements. Missing access metrics remain unknown rather than receiving SSD or HBM defaults.

lessons.name: HBF latency, transfer granularity and prefetch
lessons.shortName: HBF latency, transfer granularity and prefetch
lessons.role: Explain why matching read bandwidth does not guarantee matching request latency or useful-byte efficiency.
lessons.description: Bandwidth measures a stream; latency measures the delay before a particular dependency can proceed. NAND access and the controller’s request unit can make a small useful read consume a much larger transfer. Concurrency and prefetch can hide some delays when the next address is known early, but cannot make an unexpected dependency arrive before it is requested. Sandisk’s 2025 fact sheet explicitly qualifies its performance comparison with higher HBF latency and larger pages than HBM, using a particular internal weight-reading simulation. Writes also require their own service model: NAND programming, erasure, garbage collection and wear do not disappear behind a wider host link.
mechanism: Measure the useful request size separately from controller granularity and actual fetched bytes.
Separate first-access latency, queue time, transfer time and completion overhead.
Issue independent reads concurrently where the software knows their addresses; budget outstanding bytes and staging space.
Prefetch predictable state far enough ahead, measuring misses and wasted transfers when prediction fails.
Specify write rate, program/erase behavior, amplification and endurance for the actual configuration; do not substitute a read-bandwidth grade.

science.title: Useful-byte efficiency
science.explanation: A transaction fetches g bytes but only u are consumed before eviction. Coalescing or reuse can improve the ratio.
science.assumptions: 0 < u ≤ g, no later use of the remaining bytes; this is traffic efficiency, not a measured HBF result.

science.title: Concurrency to cover latency
science.explanation: Sustaining a target byte rate over latency L needs approximately that rate times latency in flight.
science.assumptions: Steady independent requests, adequate resources, no contention or dependency stalls; necessary capacity is not sufficient throughput proof.

specs.label: Missing HBF defaults
specs.value: Do not invent latency or page size
specs.context: Scenario inputs are hypothetical until a pinned specification or measurement supplies them.

specs.label: Reads versus writes
specs.context: Read-dominant does not mean physically read-only or unlimited endurance.

interfaces.name: Prefetch planner
interfaces.signal: Future address, issue time and useful-byte prediction

interfaces.name: Staging memory
interfaces.signal: Ready data plus occupancy and miss evidence

lessons.tradeoff: Aggressive prefetch can hide latency but consumes staging memory and bandwidth, especially when addresses or expert choices are unpredictable.
lessons.whyAI: A model that fits in a large tier can still stall if its access pattern cannot expose enough predictable parallelism.
lessons.misconception: Useful-byte efficiency is 1/16 for this synthetic access pattern; batching nearby accesses or reuse can change it.

check.question: A request fetches 16 KiB but consumes 1 KiB with no reuse. What fraction is immediately useful?
options: All of it because peak bandwidth is high
16 times the fetched volume
check.explanation: Useful-byte efficiency is 1/16 for this synthetic access pattern; batching nearby accesses or reuse can change it.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic access: 1 TB/s with 20 µs completion latency requires at least 20 MB outstanding in the simple concurrency model. A 16 KiB fetch with only 1 KiB consumed has 6.25% useful-byte efficiency. Neither latency nor granularity is an HBF product specification.
lessons.evidenceNotes: The Sandisk fact sheet’s comparison concerns internal testing/simulation of reading 8-bit pretrained Llama 3.1 405B weights, one kernel at a time on an xPU performance model. It does not establish arbitrary random reads, training writes or end-to-end serving parity. KIOXIA supports general NAND access distinctions, not HBF timing numbers.

lessons.name: Place the working set, not just the model
lessons.shortName: Place the working set, not just the model
lessons.role: Assign tensor state to tiers using lifetime, mutation, reuse distance, access size and latency requirements.
lessons.description: A model is not one undifferentiated memory allocation. Parameters, activation tiles, optimizer state, KV cache, routing metadata and checkpoints have different lifetimes and traffic. Registers and SRAM serve small, frequently reused local data; HBM supports the accelerator’s active read/write state; host DDR or LPDDR offers another capacity and compute boundary. NAND-based HBF is an emerging candidate for read-heavy near-compute state, while local and remote storage retain datasets, checkpoints and less active material. These are roles, not a universal fixed ranking: effective placement depends on the actual links, controller behavior, software and workload.
mechanism: Inventory each tensor/state object with its precision, dimensions, lifetime and mutation rate.
Identify the deadline for its next use, expected reuse distance and bytes consumed per fetch.
Reserve fast-tier space for concurrent workspaces and hot mutable state before allocating the remaining capacity to weights.
Define transfer, prefetch, eviction and consistency rules for each tier boundary, including persistent copies.
Profile misses, spills, writes and tail latency; move the object or change batching rather than judging only aggregate capacity.

science.title: Tier-capacity constraint

lessons.name: Training state across HBM, host memory and storage
lessons.shortName: Training state across HBM, host memory and storage
lessons.role: Distinguish mutable training state, recomputation, offload and durable checkpoints.
lessons.description: Training retains values for the forward pass, computes gradients and updates parameters and optimizer state. The fastest tier must therefore accommodate more than inference weights. Activation checkpointing stores selected intermediates and recomputes others; persistent checkpoints instead save restartable state outside the live execution path. State sharding changes ownership across devices, while CPU/NVMe offload moves both capacity and work across interfaces. A read-oriented flash tier cannot simply inherit the role of frequently updated optimizer or gradient storage: its write service, software support and movement schedule must be demonstrated.
mechanism: Separate parameters, gradients, master weights, optimizer moments, live activations and temporary buffers.
Set precision and sharding rules independently for each class of state.
Choose where optimizer computation occurs, keeping its mutable state and transfer requirements consistent.
Model recomputation and offload as extra work or movement rather than free capacity.
Save version-consistent durable checkpoints and measure recovery alongside steady step time.

science.title: State inventory before sharding
science.equation: Mstate = P (bw + bg + bm + bo) + A + O
science.explanation: Per-parameter byte terms represent the explicitly chosen training representation. bo includes all optimizer-state values per parameter.
science.assumptions: Dense unsharded inventory; omit absent state such as a separate master copy, then apply actual partition/replication factors by tensor class.

lessons.tradeoff: Offload and recomputation enable larger models at the cost of movement or extra arithmetic; the best choice depends on overlap and recovery requirements.

lessons.misconception: Training repeatedly updates gradient/optimizer/parameter state, so read bandwidth alone cannot characterize an appropriate tier.

Only the immutable tokenizer vocabulary

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic mixed-precision Adam inventory: 1 billion parameters × (2 weight + 2 gradient + 4 master + 8 moment bytes) = 16 GB before activations, workspace, sharding or replication. It is one representation, not a rule for every optimizer.

lessons.name: Prefill, decode and the moving KV working set
lessons.shortName: Prefill, decode and the moving KV working set
lessons.role: Place active and reusable inference state according to the execution phase and service deadline.
lessons.description: Prefill processes an input sequence and creates state for subsequent generation. Decode repeatedly generates new tokens while reading prior context and appending new KV state. Weights are reused across requests, while KV belongs to a model/version, sequence position and attention configuration. A reusable prefix can be retained or offloaded, but restoring it competes with recomputing it. Moving large KV payloads between prefill and decode nodes adds network work and coordination. Larger near-compute capacity can help only if the state is available before the next dependent operation and the placement preserves correctness.
mechanism: Identify whether the workload is prefill, decode or a mixture; record batch, context and attention architecture.
Budget the live KV payload and append/write behavior separately from weight reads.
Keep imminent mutable state accessible; choose a policy for inactive prefixes, eviction and restoration.
Compare restore transfer time with recomputation and service deadlines under actual contention.
For split serving, trace KV over its physical links and validate model/version, ownership and completion before decode uses it.

science.title: Conventional KV payload
science.equation: MKV = 2 L Hkv d b Σs Ts
science.explanation: Each stored token has key and value vectors for the specified layers and KV heads.
science.assumptions: Full conventional KV representation; no sliding windows, compression or architecture-specific state reduction. Excludes paging overhead and padding.

science.title: Restore or recompute
science.explanation: Compare this transfer lower bound with measured recomputation time and the request deadline.
science.assumptions: One aggregate transfer; includes no queueing or validation cost and assumes the cache is valid.

Yes: capacity alone establishes suitability
Yes: KV never changes during generation

lessons.name: MoE experts: resident capacity, routing and misses
lessons.shortName: MoE experts: resident capacity, routing and misses
lessons.role: Explain why sparse activation reduces arithmetic without eliminating expert storage or transfer constraints.
lessons.description: A mixture-of-experts model selects only some experts for each token, but the full parameter set still needs a valid storage and delivery strategy. A larger batch can touch many distinct experts even when each token chooses only a few. Frequently used experts may remain in fast memory; inactive expert weights can occupy another tier if the runtime can bring them in before use. Router outcomes depend on the current hidden state, so advance prediction can be imperfect. Expert parallelism also moves token activations across devices, which is a different traffic stream from fetching missing expert weights.
mechanism: Separate shared parameters, the full expert inventory and per-token selected experts.
Measure how many distinct expert weights a batch touches and which remain cached.
Account for weight misses, staging capacity and latency; track prefetch precision and wasted bytes.
Route token activations to resident experts using the actual expert-parallel topology.
Evaluate load imbalance, missed deadlines and quality-preserving routing behavior alongside throughput.

science.title: Expert-weight miss traffic
science.explanation: The set M contains distinct missing experts required during the measured reuse window; count each transferred expert once in that window.
science.assumptions: Whole expert transfer at specified stored precision, no shared/sub-tensor fetch or compression metadata; streaming changes the model.

specs.label: Two traffic streams

specs.label: Sparse activity

lessons.tradeoff: Caching popular experts saves movement but occupies scarce fast-tier space; inaccurate prefetch can consume bandwidth needed for actual misses.
lessons.whyAI: MoE capacity claims become meaningful only when routing, memory placement and interconnect scheduling can deliver selected work on time.
lessons.misconception: The union of selected experts across a batch can be much larger than the per-token selection count.

Yes: top-2 means only two experts exist
Yes: unused experts have no stored weights

lessons.name: From memory placement to network, power and cooling
lessons.shortName: From memory placement to network, power and cooling
lessons.role: Trace how a tensor-placement decision changes link demand and useful service at the hall boundary.
lessons.description: Moving state out of HBM can free capacity while creating traffic on package, CPU–GPU, PCIe, storage or network paths. Every path has its own direction, contention domain and service overhead. A larger batch may amortize weight reads while increasing KV and queueing; disaggregated serving may improve resource matching while adding KV transfers. The resulting workload changes electrical demand and heat distribution, but fixed conversion losses and idle power remain. A credible comparison closes memory, movement, compute, facility services and response-quality requirements on the same time interval.
mechanism: Start with the working-set plan and trace every moved byte across named physical interfaces.
Aggregate traffic by link and direction, separating expert-weight reads, token routing, KV movement and checkpoints.
Find a workload-rate bound from compute, memory and network demand; use a schedule to expose dependencies and overlap.
Apply measured or explicitly assumed power at the chosen IT boundary and the facility overhead at the same interval.
Report accepted outputs meeting quality and latency targets, and identify whether the constraint moved after the placement change.

science.title: Resource-normalized service bound
science.explanation: Normalize each resource to the same defined unit of work before taking the minimum.
science.assumptions: Steady aggregate upper bound, independent capacities and positive demand; omit an unused resource. Serial phases, latency and skew can lower performance.

science.title: Energy per accepted work
science.explanation: Use average IT power and accepted-work rate over the same measured interval; PUE supplies the facility boundary conversion.
science.assumptions: Stable or interval-averaged boundaries; Raccepted must be positive and enforce a defined quality/latency criterion. This is not a universal joules-per-token constant.

specs.label: Same work unit
specs.context: Define model, precision, quality and latency target.

specs.label: Boundary
specs.context: Do not mix package power with facility-wide outputs.

interfaces.signal: Accepted work, power, cooling and deployment requirements

lessons.tradeoff: Capacity offload can reduce device count but increase transfer stalls or energy elsewhere; no component metric alone predicts the net result.
lessons.whyAI: This closes the wafer → package → memory → hall → model journey through actual work rather than installed hardware totals.
lessons.misconception: A local improvement can move the bottleneck to another interface or increase work elsewhere in the system.

check.question: A placement change lowers HBM traffic but doubles remote transfers. What should be compared?
options: The complete workload at consistent quality, latency and energy boundaries
Only HBM bandwidth utilization
Only the capacity printed on the memory package
check.explanation: A local improvement can move the bottleneck to another interface or increase work elsewhere in the system.

lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic service: compute supports 300 work/s, memory 200 work/s and network 100 work/s; the simple bound is 100 work/s. Halving memory traffic alone leaves that bound unchanged. At 12 kW IT, PUE 1.2 and 90 accepted work/s, facility energy is 160 J per accepted work unit.

lessons.name: Qualify the memory system and retain useful work
lessons.shortName: Qualify the memory system and retain useful work
lessons.role: Separate component screening, integration qualification, commissioning and sustained service evidence.
lessons.description: A memory stack can pass its own tests while a system fails at a different boundary: incompatible interface options, insufficient margin under simultaneous traffic, thermal hot spots, firmware errors or an incomplete recovery path. Integration therefore checks the package, board, fabric and runtime together. Commissioning confirms that the installed site can deliver the required power, cooling, connectivity and operational controls. These gates have evidence and dates, not merely installed component counts. Once operating, corrected errors, retried reads, throttling, restarts and lost updates affect useful service and must be visible in the workload result.
mechanism: Verify component identity, test coverage, interface revision and allowed operating conditions.
Exercise the package/board memory paths under representative traffic, power and thermal conditions, preserving configuration and observed failures.
Validate error reporting, firmware/runtime responses and data correctness; distinguish corrected errors from silent corruption.
Commission facility and rack services with recovery/failure-path checks appropriate to the deployment.
Measure accepted work over time, including interruptions, retries, recovery and checkpoint loss, then feed that evidence into the next design decision.

science.title: Retained work accounting
science.explanation: Both terms use the same useful-work definition. Discarded work includes invalid results and computations that must be repeated after loss.
science.assumptions: Retries are not counted twice as retained output; accepted quality and service constraints must be specified.

specs.label: Four separate gates
specs.context: Passing one does not supply evidence for all the others.

lessons.tradeoff: Testing and redundancy add cost and time while improving confidence and service continuity; no finite test proves the absence of every future fault.
lessons.whyAI: The deployed thinking machine depends on retained correct results, not merely functional arithmetic units or announced memory capacity.

check.question: A new memory component has a published specification. What establishes system readiness?
options: Configuration-specific integration and commissioning evidence
The specification alone
A high advertised read-bandwidth grade

lessons.name: When completed work survives a restart
lessons.role: Distinguish completed, restart-durable, unfinished and lost work under a declared failure schedule.
lessons.description: A running system can finish useful steps that have not yet reached a restart-valid checkpoint. A fault preserves the last committed checkpoint, discards later volatile progress and may interrupt a partially completed step. Recovery waits and checkpoint reads consume time and energy before new work resumes. Tracking each state prevents busy hardware, completed work and durable progress from becoming the same number.
mechanism: Completed steps accumulate as volatile progress while the last committed checkpoint remains unchanged.
The example pauses execution at a whole-step boundary, writes its checkpoint and then performs an atomic commit; only that commit advances durable progress.
A fault preserves committed progress and transfers later completed and partial work to the lost-work ledger.
Repair and restore precede resumed execution. Their energy remains in the accounting, as does energy spent on work that must be repeated.
At the observation horizon, retained whole steps equal durable plus volatile completed steps. An unfinished step is excluded, and the horizon does not create a new checkpoint.

science.title: An exact work ledger for the example
science.equation: Wexec = D + V + F + L; Wretained = D + V
science.explanation: D is committed steps, V is volatile completed steps, F is the fraction of the current unfinished step, and L is cumulative discarded work equivalents. Every term uses the same whole-step workload definition.
science.assumptions: One deterministic job, atomic checkpoint commits and prescribed faults. These are model state identities; useful means completed and still retained, not accuracy, convergence or application value.

science.title: Energy per retained step
science.explanation: Facility energy integrates all active phases, including lost work, checkpoint writes, commit waits, repair and restore. Dividing by retained whole steps exposes these costs.
science.assumptions: Fixed synthetic phase powers and constant PUE. No value is reported when zero whole steps remain. Coolant heat and facility overhead are nested energy boundaries, not extra totals to add twice.

specs.label: Hand-checkable contract
specs.value: 1 s per step; one fault at 12 s
specs.context: Synthetic H7 fixture: checkpoint after 8 running seconds, 1 s write and 0.25 s commit; 2 s repair and 1 s restore.

specs.label: At the 20 s horizon
specs.context: 15.75 work equivalents executed; 2.75 discarded; no automatic checkpoint at the horizon.

specs.label: Energy boundary
specs.context: Run/checkpoint/recovery powers are 8/4/2 W. Constant scenario PUE is 1.25, not an annual measured facility rating.

interfaces.name: Mutable application state
interfaces.signal: Completed and partially completed progress under one workload contract

interfaces.name: Checkpoint storage
interfaces.signal: A complete written and committed state for restart; restore reads are distinct from writes

interfaces.name: Retained result and resource ledger
interfaces.signal: Durable, volatile, unfinished and lost work plus energy consumed over the same observation interval

lessons.tradeoff: More frequent checkpointing can reduce exposed progress but adds pauses and transfer work. The preferred interval depends on the particular workload, fault schedule and checkpoint service; this lesson establishes no universal optimum.
lessons.whyAI: Long-running training and infrastructure workloads need recoverable state. Arithmetic activity alone does not establish that progress survives interruption.
lessons.misconception: A completed computation is not necessarily durable after a restart, and losing its result does not erase the energy already spent.

check.question: In the H7 example, a checkpoint of step 8 commits at 9.25 s. Execution then runs at one step per second until a fault at 12 s. What survives immediately after the fault?
options: 8 durable steps survive; 2.75 later work equivalents are discarded.
10 whole steps survive because all completed steps are automatically durable.
10.75 useful steps survive, including the partially completed step.
check.explanation: The last valid commit protects 8 steps. The 2 completed steps and 0.75 unfinished step executed afterward are volatile, so 2.75 work equivalents move to the lost-work ledger.

lessons.learningObjective: Calculate retained and restart-durable work from an explicit checkpoint/fault timeline, close the work and energy ledgers, and explain the limit of the result.
lessons.engineeringExample: Synthetic H7: run 0–8 s; write 8–9 s; commit 9–9.25 s; run 9.25–12 s; repair 12–14 s; restore 14–15 s; run 15–20 s. Retained progress is 8 + 5 = 13 whole steps; executed work is 8 + 2.75 + 5 = 15.75 equivalents. IT energy is 15.75×8 + 1.25×4 + 3×2 = 137 J; facility energy is 1.25×137 = 171.25 J.
lessons.evidenceNotes: The source documents checkpoint completion and valid restart, not this atomic timing or its invented numerical inputs. H7 executes with the included teaching runner; the current browser hall controls do not expose every small fixture rate. No human specialist review, instructor observation or learning efficacy result is claimed.
